recipes.title: Fermented Plant Juice (FPJ)
recipes.description: FPJ captures vegetative growth hormones and soluble nutrition from fast-growing plant tips via brown-sugar osmosis. For peppers, it is the primary liquid ‘food’ while plants are building leaves and roots before heavy flowering.

ingredients.name: Vigorous shoot tips
ingredients.notes: Comfrey, sweet potato vine, or moringa—no disease

steps.instruction: Harvest tips near dawn when turgor is high; skip rinsing to preserve epiphytic microbes.
Chop to thumb-length pieces to rupture cells without liquefying the mash.
Alternate thin layers of plant and sugar, pressing firmly to exclude air.
steps.tips: Liquid should begin weeping within a day.

steps.instruction: Cover with cloth; store warm-shade; date the batch.
When bubbling slows and aroma is tangy-sweet, strain through muslin.
Bottle amber liquid in glass with head space; refrigerate only if indoor temps exceed ~85°F.
Compost the marc or fold into an IMO3 pile to close the loop.

tips: Pull back FPJ as clusters set— lingering vegetative pushes delay pod fill in some cultivars.
Pair FPJ foliars with LAB drench on different nights to keep leaf surfaces from overloading.
safety_notes: Discard ferments dominated by continuous black, foul anaerobic slime or acrid ammonia with no balancing sour-sweet note.
recipes.application_frequency: Every 7–10 days during vegetative growth

recipes.title: Fermented Fruit Juice (FFJ)
recipes.description: FFJ uses ripe fruit and brown sugar to yield a reproductive-stage liquid rich in sugars, acids, and aromatics. It complements mineral inputs once peppers move from canopy building into flowering, fruit set, and ripening.

steps.instruction: Remove stems, cores, and bruises; dice fruit for dense packing.
Layer fruit and sugar, pressing each layer to express juice.
Cover with cloth; monitor overflow during warm weather.
After activity slows, strain through muslin; discard marc to hot compost.
Bottle, date, and store cool-dark; smell should stay fruity-acidic.
Optional second soak of marc in light brine for weaker secondary press—label separately.

tips: Begin FFJ as buds appear; taper FPJ so nitrogen does not swamp fruit loading.
Mix weaker FFJ with WCA during rapid fruit expansion to buffer calcium demand.
safety_notes: Discard ferments dominated by continuous black, foul anaerobic slime or acrid ammonia with no balancing sour-sweet note.
recipes.application_frequency: Every 7–14 days from bloom through ripening

recipes.title: Fish Amino Acid (FAA)
recipes.description: Ferments fish scraps under brown sugar to supply amino nitrogen and trace proteins without synthetic ammonium shock. It belongs in the vegetative toolbox but always heavily diluted and rotated with microbial inputs.

ingredients.name: Fresh fish scraps
ingredients.notes: Heads & frames; keep chilled until pack

steps.instruction: Dice fish small; alternate equal layers, pressing out air voids.
Seal with burp schedule or fermentation lock—never rigid glass without head-room.
Burp weekly at first; later monthly; liquid rises as solids collapse.
Mature FAA smells savory-fermented, not purely septic.
steps.tips: If uncertain, wait longer or dilute more.

steps.instruction: Strain; bottle amber liquid; solids bury in active compost—away from waterways.

tips: Separate FAA days from heavy IMO liquid drenches so biology can process nitrogen gradually.
Older FAA is milder—mark vintage and expect to stretch dilution on sensitive peppers.
safety_notes: Pressurized jars can rupture—never hermetically seal a warming batch.
Discard ferments dominated by continuous black, foul anaerobic slime or acrid ammonia with no balancing sour-sweet note.
recipes.application_rate: Begin ~1:1,200 for seedlings; vigorous adults sometimes accept 1:500
recipes.application_frequency: 10–14 day intervals during leafy growth phases
best_for: Chlorosis correction when biology is already active

recipes.title: Lactic Acid Bacteria Serum (LAB)
recipes.fermentation_time: 3–7 days rice wash; optional milk curd 1 day
recipes.description: LAB serum harvests lactobacilli from rice-wash fermentation or from milk curds, then stabilizes the clarified fluid with sugar for shelf life. In humid pepper houses it keeps anaerobic pockets in check and complements IMO drenches without synthetic fungicides.

steps.instruction: Perform a gentle first rinse of rice; decant the cloudy fraction into a jar.
Loosely cover; wait until the liquid sours pleasantly (~3 days).
Strain rice wash liquid; optionally inoculate milk to curd and harvest whey.
steps.tips: Stop milk path if curds smell off.

steps.instruction: Collect the translucent fraction beneath foam or curds.
Mix 1:1 with brown sugar to stabilize; stir until dissolved.
Bottle refrigerated; label concentration date.
Field-apply at extreme dilution—start at 1:2,000 on seedlings.

tips: Chlorinated municipal water kills LAB—use filtered or rested water overnight.
Alternate with FFJ/WCA sprays so acids do not accumulate on waxy leaves in one pass.
safety_notes: Do not aerosolize concentrated acid without PPE; dilute before spraying.
Discard ferments dominated by continuous black, foul anaerobic slime or acrid ammonia with no balancing sour-sweet note.
recipes.application_frequency: Weekly during establishment; monthly once soils stabilize

recipes.title: Oriental Herbal Nutrient (OHN)
recipes.description: OHN macerates five traditional botanicals through alternating alcohol and vinegar phases to produce a resilient immune-support tonic. Small amounts travel into almost every maintenance spray because it buffers stress during Florida heat snaps and wind events.

ingredients.name: Angelica, cinnamon, licorice, ginger, garlic (fresh/dried per CGNF guidance)

steps.instruction: Chop herbs roughly; pack each botanical separately—never moldy inputs.
Pour alcohol to cover; seal lightly; store dark, labeling alcohol pulls.
Drain alcohol fraction; reserve; begin vinegar soak per schedule.
Repeat alcohol/vinegar alternations until plant cellulose surrenders color.
Combine equal finished extracts (or prescribed ratios) into master OHN.
Rest combined OHN; decant clear fraction; sugar-stabilize if protocol demands.
Bottle dark glass; OHN improves with age when stored cool.
Always shake before dilute use so oils redistribute.
Never smell-test directly from concentrate—waft vapors to avoid ethanol inhalation.
Document batch codes for traceability in nursery QA logs.

tips: Use fractions of a teaspoon per gallon on maintenance sprays—OHN is potent.
If licensing or alcohol sourcing blocks you, purchase inspected OHN and log supplier COA.
safety_notes: High-proof alcohol and vapors are flammable—no open flame.
Potassium hydroxide and hot oils cause severe burns—nitrile gloves, eye protection, ventilation, and no aluminum vessels.
recipes.application_rate: ~¾ tsp OHN per gallon when paired with FPJ + BRV maintenance cocktail
recipes.application_frequency: Every 10–12 days alongside normal KNF rotations

recipes.title: Homemade Brown Rice Vinegar (BRV)
recipes.description: BRV is slow dual-stage vinegar from whole brown rice—first sugar wine, then acetification. It extracts eggshell calcium for WCA/WCP and appears in nearly every KNF spray as a gentle acidifier and mildew deterrent.

ingredients.name: Food-grade storage barrel or glass demijohn
ingredients.notes: Acetobacter needs air but limits fruit fly

steps.instruction: Steam rice fluffy; cool; inoculate with koji or trusted wine yeast to saccharify.
Maintain anaerobic alcohol stage until specific gravity stabilizes.
Introduce cellulose-wrapped mother or raw vinegar back-slop; introduce oxygen gently.
Hold 60–85°F with stable oxygen; acetification may take months.
Taste monthly; stop at balanced sour—not harsh industrial acetate burn.
Pull finished BRV; pasteurize only if required by your SOP—otherwise raw vinegar for living extracts.
Age in glass; acid matures; record each pull’s pH.

tips: If home BRV stalls, source verified brown rice vinegar commercially while your batch ages.
Use the same vintage for each extraction batch so WCA saturation rates stay predictable.
safety_notes: Discard ferments dominated by continuous black, foul anaerobic slime or acrid ammonia with no balancing sour-sweet note.
recipes.application_rate: 1:1,000 in sprays (component) or full-strength as extract solvent only
recipes.application_frequency: Component of maintenance sprays every 10–12 days

recipes.title: Water-Soluble Calcium (WCA)
recipes.description: WCA dissolves calcium carbonate from roasted eggshells into brown rice vinegar, creating a foliar-available calcium spray. It targets blossom-end rot risk and fruit cracking when rapid cell expansion outruns internal calcium supply in peppers.

steps.instruction: Dry-clean shells; roast until lightly tan—not chalk-white ash.
Break shells to pea size to increase surface area.
Add to vinegar slowly; observe bubbling CO₂—vent if foam threatens overflow.
Rest capped with cloth 7–10 days until bubbling stops.
Strain; label saturated WCA; store dark/cool.
Confirm no grit in spray lines—filter twice for greenhouse foggers.

tips: Apply after peak transpiration (dusk) to maximize passive uptake through young fruits.
Rotate nights with seawater sprays so salinity and calcium stay balanced.
safety_notes: Acid + shells release CO₂ in closed jars—never seal glass tightly during initial reaction.
recipes.application_rate: 1:1,000 foliar typical (see kitchen measure tables for your tank)
recipes.application_frequency: 7–10 days during rapid pod expansion

recipes.title: Water-Soluble Calcium Phosphate (WCP)
recipes.description: WCP solubilizes phosphate from properly burned bones using BRV, supporting flowering, root flush, and seed maturity. It complements WCA as peppers transition from vegetative mass into reproductive allocation.

steps.instruction: Low-temperature burn bones until brittle, chalk-white-gray—not charcoal.
Cool; crack bones; pack loosely in glass or ceramic—not metal with long soaks.
Cover with BRV; vent CO₂ if foaming.
Soak 7–10 days; top vinegar if evaporation exposes bone.
Strain liquid WCP; store labeled; solids may re-soak weaker.

tips: Apply during pre-bloom and early fruit set—not a substitute for soil P tests if deficiency is extreme.
Never dump raw vinegar concentrates into irrigation reservoirs—mix dilute first.
safety_notes: Burning bones releases odors/particulates—PPE + neighbor courtesy.
recipes.application_frequency: Every 10–14 days during flowering and early fruit

recipes.title: Clean Ocean Seawater Dilution (Mineral Drench)
recipes.description: Well-sourced seawater contributes trace minerals that strengthen fruit quality and can help manage certain fungal threats when properly diluted. On Florida farms it must be captured away from harmful algal blooms or urban plume runoff.

steps.instruction: Sample only during calm, clear tide windows; avoid red-tide advisories.
Filter through coffee mesh to remove debris and plankton.
Dilute start 1:30 for first ripening passes; tighten only with observation.
Apply as evening foliar or drench when stomata are open but sun won’t bake salt.
Log electrical conductivity if fertigating so totals stay within pepper tolerance.

tips: Advance dilution strength gradually as pods mature—never jump from 1:40 to 1:10 overnight.
Pause seawater if margins desiccate—pair with fresh OM mulches.
safety_notes: Salinity burns tissue when concentrated—always pre-dilute and spot-test a branch.
recipes.application_frequency: Every 10–14 days through final swell

recipes.title: Fermented Seawater (FSW)
recipes.description: Fermented seawater marries diluted seawater with rice-wash microbes and a small FPJ fraction so minerals arrive with active biology. Growers on the humid Gulf and Atlantic coasts use it preventively during anthracnose pressure on ripe pods.

steps.instruction: Build base dilution seawater per ripening plan (start weakest).
Add rice wash or diluted LAB before oils or acids hit the tank.
Add FPJ last; stir gently; avoid whipping excess foam.
Allow warm-weather ferments 12–24 h; extend if overcast or cool.
steps.tips: Smell stays sea-mineral, not sour milk.

steps.instruction: Strain if precipitate forms; spray dusk or dawn.
Clean tank jets after salt sprays to prevent clogging.

tips: Alternate FSW nights with JS/JHS programs so surfaces aren’t coated daily with minerals + sulfur.
Use greenhouse staging—first road-test low tunnels before whole block sprays.
safety_notes: Same salinity cautions as plain seawater; never spray drought-stressed plants at midday.
recipes.application_rate: Dilution anchored to seawater recipe; biology additives stay trace
recipes.application_frequency: Preventive every 10–14 days during humid fruiting

recipes.title: IMO Stage 1 — Forest Floor Rice Capture
recipes.description: Capture indigenous microbes from locally adapted leaf litter using steamed rice as a substrate. It is the start of every IMO sequence and should reflect your watershed’s fungal:bacterial balance—not bagged off-site inoculants.

steps.instruction: Locate healthy forest edge or old-growth understory free of chemical drift.
Steam rice to al dente; cool to blood temperature.
Place handful on bamboo tray/box; bury lightly under native litter; cover loosely.
Return in 3–5 days; IMO1 is ready when fungal hyphae dominate with clean white bloom.
Harvest only what you need; leave biomass to regenerate microflora.
Document GPS + date for traceability.

tips: Never equate IMO with random bagged EM—traceability to your biome matters.
If molds discolor, consult local extension before repeating collection from the same cluster.
safety_notes: Wild collection respects land access rules; tick / wildlife awareness in understory work.
recipes.application_frequency: Per crop phenology—often weekly establishment then monthly

recipes.title: IMO Stage 2 — Sugar-Stabilized Liquid
recipes.description: Preserved IMO1 myceliated rice with brown sugar draws osmotic liquid teeming with captured microbes. This concentrate becomes the inoculant backbone for field expansions and compost integrations.

steps.instruction: Combine captured IMO1 rice 1:1 by weight with brown sugar.
Pack tightly to exclude air; cover breathable.
After 7 days, collect dense syrup—this is your IMO2 stock.
Decant; bottle dark glass; label potency date.
Store cool; use aliquots for expansion instead of reopening whole stock weekly.
Sanitize transfer tools with boiling water—not bleach—which kills target biota.

tips: Never equate IMO with random bagged EM—traceability to your biome matters.
If molds discolor, consult local extension before repeating collection from the same cluster.
safety_notes: Wild collection respects land access rules; tick / wildlife awareness in understory work.
recipes.application_frequency: Per crop phenology—often weekly establishment then monthly

recipes.title: IMO Stage 3 — Aerobic Field Compost Activation
recipes.description: Turns liquid IMO into low-temperature compost piles that expand microbial mass on carbon stacks. Stage three is where structure and moisture discipline matter most in Florida afternoon storms.

steps.instruction: Form loose windrow/pile using local carbon, nitrogen, mineral amendments per farm plan.
Dilute IMO2 1:500–1:1,000 into chlorine-free water; even distribution matters.
Turn pile when core hits ~50°C (122°F) max: do not exceed KNF thermal guidance.
Maintain field moisture like a wrung sponge—never anaerobic slime for long.
Harvest friable, sweet-earth smelling compost.
Sieve if needed for potting integration.

tips: Never equate IMO with random bagged EM—traceability to your biome matters.
If molds discolor, consult local extension before repeating collection from the same cluster.
safety_notes: Wild collection respects land access rules; tick / wildlife awareness in understory work.
recipes.application_frequency: Per crop phenology—often weekly establishment then monthly

recipes.title: IMO Stage 4 — Finished Soil Amendment Blend
recipes.description: Combines matured IMO3 with mineral inputs, FAA/OHN/Fish ferments, and local soil to create a stable inoculated amendment. It is the product many growers bucket onto beds, container mixes, and transplant holes.

steps.instruction: Combine matured IMO3 with equal parts indigenous topsoil + compost.
Add small FAA, OHN, WCP/WCA concentrates per soil test targets.
Integrate biochar or crushed shell if pH adjustments demand buffering.
Mix to uniform color; moisture ~40%.
Cure 7–14 days under shade cloth; turn twice weekly.
Apply as topdress or incorporate pre-plant.

tips: Never equate IMO with random bagged EM—traceability to your biome matters.
If molds discolor, consult local extension before repeating collection from the same cluster.
safety_notes: Wild collection respects land access rules; tick / wildlife awareness in understory work.
recipes.application_frequency: Per crop phenology—often weekly establishment then monthly

recipes.title: IMO Stage 5 — Fish-Enhanced Microbial Expansion (Optional)
recipes.description: Optional fifth stage introduces fish hydrolysate fractions to push fungal energy in specific tree/shrub contexts; adapt cautiously for annual peppers to avoid nitrogen spike timing errors.

steps.instruction: Start only after mastering IMO4; source sustainable fish hydrolysate fractions.
Blend trace amounts into compost windrow to steer fungal consortium.
Monitor nitrogen release so pepper leaf tips don’t burn—pull back if cupping appears.
Restrict to perennial windbreak mulch unless annual beds expressly need fungal dominance.
Document application rates; not every pepper rotation benefits.

tips: Never equate IMO with random bagged EM—traceability to your biome matters.
If molds discolor, consult local extension before repeating collection from the same cluster.
safety_notes: Wild collection respects land access rules; tick / wildlife awareness in understory work.
recipes.application_frequency: Per crop phenology—often weekly establishment then monthly

recipes.title: JADAM Microorganism Solution (JMS)
recipes.description: JMS is JADAM’s simplified aerobic microbe broth that activates indigenous soil life without the lengthy IMO sequence. It fits nursery operations that need fast-turn biology between short pepper rotations.

steps.instruction: Boil starch water; cool to blood temp; dissolve pinch salt if protocol demands.
Whisk in compost/leaf mold until evenly turbid.
Aerate 12 hours with aquarium pump or swirl hourly.
Strain through mesh; dilute 1:100–1:500 for field sprays.
Use fresh batches—JMS isn’t a months-long concentrate.

tips: Good for bridging between KNF heavy ferments when time is tight.
Log smell: malty/earthy good; rotten eggs means anaerobic failure.
safety_notes: Small-batch odors attract wildlife—secure greenhouse vents overnight.
recipes.application_frequency: Weekly for 3 weeks post-transplant, then monthly

recipes.title: JADAM Wetting Agent (JWA)
recipes.description: JWA is a potassium-saponified vegetable oil soap that helps sprays coat waxy pepper leaves evenly. Always add JWA last in the tank after diluting sulfur or oils to avoid locked-in emulsions.

steps.instruction: Dissolve KOH in water outdoors—exothermic, caustic fumes.
Add oil slowly while stirring until thick soap forms.
Let saponify until pH stabilizes per strip logging.
Dilute stock into labeled bottles; store cool.
Foam-test in a jar of your spray water before batching expensive inputs.

tips: Typical spray use ~1–2 mL/L—last ingredient into the tank.
Hard well water may need citric pretreatment—test jar foam stability.
safety_notes: Potassium hydroxide and hot oils cause severe burns—nitrile gloves, eye protection, ventilation, and no aluminum vessels.
recipes.application_rate: ≈1–2 mL per liter of spray solution
recipes.application_frequency: Whenever using JS, JHS, neem, or mineral suspensions
best_for: Soft-bodied insect washes combined with JHS

recipes.title: JADAM Sulfur (JS) Fungicide
recipes.description: JS dissolves elemental sulfur with KOH to create a powerful organic fungicide without lime-sulfur’s steel corrosion. Pepper growers lean on JS + JWA during Florida’s mildew windows but must respect heat/humidity phytotoxicity thresholds.

steps.instruction: Combine KOH + sulfur + water gradually; expect heat—stir non-aluminum pot.
Dissolve fully to wine-dark solution without grit.
Bottle aged concentrate; label molar-ish batch strength.
Never mix the same day with copper sprays—phytotoxic pairings.
Store concentrate in opaque HDPE, log pH monthly, and shake before any dilution so suspended sulfur stays even.
steps.tips: Replace stock if crystals precipitate unevenly after cool storage.

tips: Dilute 100:1 to 200:1 for maintenance; tighten only on confirmed infection.
Spray early/late—never >95°F canopy temps.
safety_notes: Potassium hydroxide and hot oils cause severe burns—nitrile gloves, eye protection, ventilation, and no aluminum vessels.
recipes.application_rate: Typically 100:1 to 500:1 dilution from concentrate (see severity tables)
recipes.application_frequency: At most every 7 days during active mildew—rotate modes of action

recipes.title: JADAM Herbal Solution (JHS)
recipes.description: JHS ferments repellant / insecticidal herbs into a stable extract used soft or hot depending on pest pressure. Farm-scaled batches respect USDA organic approved species lists—always verify before shipping peppers.

ingredients.name: Fresh aromatic herbs (mint, mugwort, hot peppers, etc.)

steps.instruction: Wash only if contaminant risk; otherwise wildcrafted herbs prefer dry-brush cleaning.
Chop fine; alternate herb and sugar layers.
Ferment until aromatic syrup stabilizes (3–7 days warm).
Strain; stabilize; store refrigerated if your bay runs >80°F nights.
Dilute with JWA for coverage; rotate weekly with JS to avoid resistance.

tips: Spot-test each cultivar—superhots sometimes show marginal burn when oils concentrate.
Night applications preserve pollinators on adjacent rows.
safety_notes: Eye/skin sensitivity to hot pepper extracts—use goggles when macerating.
recipes.application_rate: Often 200:1 stock dilution window—tighten only with scouting logs
recipes.application_frequency: Weekly during outbreaks; back to 14 days when clean

recipes.title: Pyroligneous Acid (Wood Vinegar / WS)
recipes.description: Wood vinegar is the condensed smoke fraction from controlled biomass pyrolysis—distinct from culinary smoke flavorings. In disciplined KNF it is used in tiny dilutions for soil biology signaling—not choked into reservoir irrigation unchecked.

steps.instruction: Only proceed if local regulations and insurance cover small-batch pyrolysis.
Fraction crude pyroligneous acid into light/middle/heavy cuts during cooling.
Age 3–6 months vented so harsh phenolics mellow.
Dilute 1:500–1:1,000 for exploratory soil drenches; never foliar-heavy raw.
If sourcing retail pyroligneous acid, verify agricultural grade—not barbecue smokefluid.

tips: Consider purchasing vetted agricultural wood vinegar before building kilns solely for peppers.
Great for shifting bacterial slag soils toward fungal balance when combined with carbon.
safety_notes: Fire + carbon monoxide hazard—no improvised indoor attempts.
Potassium hydroxide and hot oils cause severe burns—nitrile gloves, eye protection, ventilation, and no aluminum vessels.
recipes.application_rate: Trace—begin near 1:1,000 drench trials on a sacrificial row
recipes.application_frequency: Quarterly at most unless soil logs justify repetition

recipes.title: JADAM Liquid Fertilizer from Green Manure (JLF)
recipes.description: JLF-style green manure ferments dissolve nitrogen and minerals from cover crops and weeds into a liquid accessible for fertigation or foliar. It aligns with JADAM’s cost discipline while still closing nutrient loops on-farm.

steps.instruction: Shred biomass; pack vessel; exclude air gaps
Add water until submerged; stir daily first week.
When aroma steadies sweet-sour, strain press solids.
Dilute 1:50–1:200 onto soil; avoid heavy foliar unless filtered finely.
Return solids to windrow.

tips: Rotate green manure species to diversify amino profiles year to year.
Night irrigation reduces phototoxicity where particulates remain.
safety_notes: Discard ferments dominated by continuous black, foul anaerobic slime or acrid ammonia with no balancing sour-sweet note.
recipes.application_rate: Highly variable—start weak on sandier soils
recipes.application_frequency: Weekly for hungry rotations; back off when sap tests climb

recipes.title: Rice Wash Water Capture
recipes.description: The first cloudy rice rinse is a low-tech microbial broth starter used across KNF and JADAM contexts. It inoculates seedlings, primes compost teas, and extends LAB without expensive starters.

steps.instruction: Rinse organic rice once with body-temp water—capture only that first cloud.
Dilute into irrigation or sprinkle trays immediately or ferment 24 h lightly covered.
Use within 48 h or route into LAB mother jars.
Never rely on fifth+ rinses—mostly starch without biology.
Log smell + turbidity to train crew eyes.

tips: Treat living teas like dairy—time and temperature dominantly affect quality.
Keep logs tying each batch to cultivars sprayed for traceability.
safety_notes: Verify PPE for dusts when handling dry compost in humid houses.
recipes.application_rate: Soil drench typically 10–20 gal finished tea / 1000 sq ft—adjust per media
recipes.application_frequency: Monthly maintenance or weekly recovery after stress events

recipes.title: KNF Maintenance Foliar (FPJ + OHN + BRV)
recipes.description: The backbone KNF maintenance mix stacks vegetative nutrition (FPJ) with herbal resilience (OHN) and mild acidification (BRV). Use it only when plants show healthy uptake—never as a daily firehose.

steps.instruction: Blend equal micro-doses of FPJ, OHN, and BRV into the spray tank at target total dilution (often ~1:500 each).
Fill tank with clean, low-EC water; verify pH and EC baselines.
Spot-test a few flagship plants before house-wide deployment.
Spray dusk or dawn under calm air; stop if margins crinkle overnight.
Rinse nozzles—sugars ferment in lines if idle.

tips: Treat living teas like dairy—time and temperature dominantly affect quality.
Keep logs tying each batch to cultivars sprayed for traceability.
safety_notes: Verify PPE for dusts when handling dry compost in humid houses.
recipes.application_rate: Soil drench typically 10–20 gal finished tea / 1000 sq ft—adjust per media
recipes.application_frequency: Monthly maintenance or weekly recovery after stress events

recipes.title: Seed Priming Soak (WCA + OHN + LAB)
recipes.description: Combines dilute mineral calcium, herbal immune tone, and lactic biology for a controlled seed soak before sowing superhots. It tightens germination curves without synthetic seed treatments barred on farm.

steps.instruction: Assemble mature inputs diluted warmer than final soak EC target.
Soak seeds 6–12 h depending on thickness—never exceed pepper tolerance.
Drain on sterile towel; air dry sowing window ~1 h to prevent rot.
Sow immediately into sterile media; maintain diurnal temps per cultivar.
Log emergence % vs untreated controls for QA.

tips: Treat living teas like dairy—time and temperature dominantly affect quality.
Keep logs tying each batch to cultivars sprayed for traceability.
safety_notes: Verify PPE for dusts when handling dry compost in humid houses.
recipes.application_rate: Soil drench typically 10–20 gal finished tea / 1000 sq ft—adjust per media
recipes.application_frequency: Monthly maintenance or weekly recovery after stress events

recipes.title: Aerated Compost Tea (Non-Thermal Extract)
recipes.description: Active aeration multiplies beneficial bacteria/fungi from verified compost into a 24–36 h living extract. Use it as a soil drench—not always a miracle foliar on waxy pepper leaves without adjuvants.

steps.instruction: Start with lab-tested compost low in human pathogens.
Bag in 400-micron mesh; suspend in chlorine-free water with vigorous bubbles.
Feed modest microbe foods (unsulfured molasses) only if protocol demands.
Brew 24–36 h; stop before anaerobic biofilm slicks dominate.
Use within 4 h of ceasing aeration.

tips: Treat living teas like dairy—time and temperature dominantly affect quality.
Keep logs tying each batch to cultivars sprayed for traceability.
safety_notes: Verify PPE for dusts when handling dry compost in humid houses.
recipes.application_rate: Soil drench typically 10–20 gal finished tea / 1000 sq ft—adjust per media
recipes.application_frequency: Monthly maintenance or weekly recovery after stress events

recipes.title: Static Compost Extract (Passive Steep)
recipes.description: Passive extraction steeps finished compost without aerators—ideal when power fails or travel interrupts brewing. Microbial diversity is lower than active tea but still valuable for soil drenches.

steps.instruction: Site system; manage vectors (leachate, flies, rodents) per county rules.
Balance C:N and moisture targets for the method selected.
Monitor temperature and/or worm biomass depending on system.
Harvest stable product; screen to media grade for potting mixes.
Document analyticals if selling castings or compost externally.
Integrate with greenhouse sanitation SOP.

tips: Never rely on one compost method—cohort systems hedge equipment failure.
Match particle size to drip emitters if fertigating extracts.
safety_notes: Heat exhaustion during summer pile turns—crew hydration + shade planning.
recipes.application_rate: Incorporate per soil test and crop rotation plan
recipes.application_frequency: Whenever organic matter drops below management targets

steps.instruction: Site system; manage vectors (leachate, flies, rodents) per county rules.

Monitor temperature and/or worm biomass depending on system.
